metadata.file_name: Student well-being and mathematical literacy performance in PISA 2018  a machine-learning approach.pdf
metadata.title: Student well-being and mathematical literacy performance in PISA 2018: a machine-learning approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a secondary analysis of the OECD PISA 2018 database for Spain, focusing on students aged 15–16. The analytic sample is described as the Spanish student body participating in PISA 2018 (35,943), with no explicit mention of applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the machine-learning or multilevel modeling steps. Because the manuscript does not report any weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate design method (e.g., BRR/jackknife), weighting cannot be confirmed; the reported modeling pipeline (training/validation split, imputation, scaling, ML hyperparameter tuning, and multilevel random-intercept regression) appears to be implemented without documented complex-survey weight handling. The main preprocessing steps explicitly reported are multiple imputation via chained equations, centering/scaling of continuous predictors, and checking for near-zero variance predictors.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Spanish student body that participated in PISA 2018 (students aged 15–16). The response variable (mathematical literacy) is based on ten plausible values; the authors processed missing values using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) and then randomly split the data into training (70%) and validation sets. For the first two objectives, decision tree and random forest models were repeated/selected across plausible values, with plausible value number 8 chosen based on lowest RMSE. For the multilevel hierarchical linear models, the nested structure (students level 1; schools level 2) was modeled with random intercepts, and categorical predictors were dichotomised (with additional CART-based dichotomisation for selected discrete quantitative variables).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (mathematical literacy; plausible values; Spain; students aged 15–16)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Decision Tree — selected plausible value 8 by lowest RMSE (RMSE = 82.985; min observations per node = 25; max depth = 3; min terminal node size = 100). Random Forest — selected plausible value 8 by lowest RMSE (RMSE = 75.579; 401 trees; max depth = 25).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics data (mathematical literacy; plausible values; Spain; students aged 15–16), the study leveraged Talk to mother’s partner, Talk to father’s partner, Friends days after school, Student ESCS, and Average school ESCS to predict Mathematical literacy (PISA plausible value 8), finding that Random Forest achieved lower estimation error than regression trees (RMSE 75.579 vs. 82.985). This indicates that social well-being-related communication and peer time—alongside socioeconomic context—are predictive of higher mathematical literacy, suggesting that schools should target social-emotional supports to improve math outcomes, while noting that the study is predictive (not causal) and does not document complex-survey weight use.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (mathematical literacy; multilevel random-intercept models; Spain; students aged 15–16)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel HLM (random-intercept): Model 1 (socioeconomic context) explains 61.004% of variability; Model 2 (Model 1 + 15 well-being variables) increases explained variance to 66.912% (additional +6%). Key coefficients: ESCS +23.101; Average school ESCS +25.122. Social well-being effects in Model 2: talking to mother’s/father’s partner −16.102/−14.687; talking to teacher +20.757; friends 5 days/week −20.494; PE classes zero/3+ days −31.573.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics data (mathematical literacy; multilevel random-intercept models; Spain; students aged 15–16), the study leveraged Student ESCS, Average school ESCS, and social well-being communication variables (e.g., talking to mother’s/father’s partner and talking to teachers) to predict Mathematical literacy, finding that adding student well-being variables increased explained variance from 61.004% to 66.912% and that several social well-being indicators had statistically significant associations with math scores. This indicates that strengthening social-emotional relationships and communication supports in school and family contexts may narrow socioeconomic- and context-related math gaps, though causality cannot be inferred from this cross-sectional design.

data.outcome_summary: The study conducts a secondary analysis of PISA 2018 mathematics (mathematical literacy) for Spain, using students aged 15–16 (N=35,943). The dependent variable is mathematical literacy represented by ten plausible values; the authors imputed missing data using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), then trained decision tree and random forest models on a 70/30 training/validation split and selected plausible value 8 based on lowest RMSE. Random Forest outperformed regression trees in estimation error (RMSE 75.579 vs. 82.985). For the multilevel component, hierarchical linear models with random intercepts at the school level showed that socioeconomic context alone explained 61.004% of variability, while adding 15 well-being variables increased explained variance to 66.912% (ICC reduced from 15.014% to 5.656%). The paper reports associations and predictive performance but does not establish causality and does not document complex-survey weight application.
